records.rawDisplayText:
Members of the genus Flavobacterium such as F. columnare, F. psychrophilum, F. collinsii, F. tructae, F. branchiophilum, F. hydatis, F. succinicans, F. flevense, F. chilense and F. aquatile are Gram-negative aerobic rods, that demonstrates a widespread distribution in different habitats including diseased fish [9]. Of these, F. columnare which causes columnaris disease, is one of the first documented fish diseases known worldwide. Discoloration, gill necrosis, and fin and skin erosion were the most noticeable external symptoms of disease in fish. Recently, the strain of F. columnare affecting tilapia was reclassified as F. oreochromis [19].

records.rawDisplayText:
Fish tenacibaculosis is caused by several different 
members of the Tenacibaculum genus, including T. 
maritimum, T. piscium, T. dicentrarchi, T. gallaicum, T. 
discolor, T. finnmarkense, T. soleae and very recently 
isolated T. ovolyticum [20]. These are Gram-negative, 
marine, filamentous bacteria that cause fish diseases 
characterized by symptoms such as necrosis, erosion 
of the mouth, superficial skin lesions, and a lack of 
coloration in internal organs. Among these T. maritimum
has been associated with mortality of numerous marine 
and anadromous fish species, both in their natural habitats 
and in captivity [10]. Fish Lactococcosis caused by Grampositive Lactococcus garvieae [21] and the more recently 
identified L. petauri [22] is an emerging bacterial infection 
characterized by hemorrhagic septicemia. Isolation of L. 
piscium from diseased rainbow, trout was the first and sole 
report of it as a fish pathogen [23].
翻译,并写入末尾

records.rawDisplayText:
Important fish pathogenic Bacteria from the genus
Acinetobacter such as A. baumannii, A. johnsonii, A. pittii,
A. lwoffii, and A. junii are Gram-negative, strictly aerobic,
non-fermentative, and non-motile rods. Symptoms such
as exophthalmia, dark color of the body, and occasional
ulcers on the external part of the body of the infected fish
are commonly observed. They are ubiquitously distributed
in natural environments and frequently encountered in
both marine and freshwater fish populations such as
diseased common carp (Cyprinus carpio), channel catfish
(Ictalurus punctatus), righteye flounder (Poecilopsetta
plinthus), rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), zebrafish
(Barchydanio rerio), blunt snout bream (Megalobrama
amblycephala), south Asian carp (Labeo catla) [12].

records.rawDisplayText:
Three important fish pathogens, of the genus Nocardia
namely N. seriolae, N. asteroids, and N. salmonicida are
responsible for fish nocardiosis which is a granulomatous,
chronic bacterial disease. Bacteria in this genus are nonmotile, Gram-positive, and aerobic. Common clinical
indicators of infection in fish include skin ulcers along with
several white nodule-like structures on gills, as well as in
the kidney, liver, spleen, head, and several other parts of
the body. Nocardiosis infection is reported both in marine
as well as freshwater fish species which includes northern
snakehead (Channa argus) in Korea, yellow tail (Seriola
quinqueradiata) in Japan, pompano (Trachinotus ovatus),
largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides), tiger perch
(Terapon jarbua) and large yellow croaker (Larimichthys
crocea) in China and chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus
tshawytscha) in Europe and USA [13].

records.rawDisplayText:
Shewanella spp. is recognized as an opportunistic
pathogen affecting both humans and fish, exhibiting a
broad spectrum of clinical manifestations. Among the
noteworthy members of the genus reported in fish include
S. putrefaciens, S. xiamenensis S. oncorhynchi, S. baltica,
S. morhuae, and S. algae. Shewanella spp. are saprophytic,
rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacteria causing gill and skin
necrosis, along with ulcerative lesions in the infected fish  
[15]. The genus Mycobacteria, causing mycobacteriosis
in fish and other animals are Gram-positive, aerobic, and
non-motile bacilli. Over fifteen mycobacterial species have
been obtained from ornamental, cultivated, and wild fish
species. Researchers have isolated more than fifteen different
mycobacterial species from cultured, ornamental, and
wild fish species. Among them, Mycobacterium chelonae,
M. marinum, and M. fortuitum are the prominent ones
reported in several diseased fish species such as guppies
(Poecilia reticulata), yellowtail (Seriola quinqueradiata),
koi carp (Cyprinus  rubrofuscus), Japanese pufferfish
(Takifugu rubripes), gilthead sea bream (Sparus aurata),
Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), red drum (Sciaenops
ocellatus) and European seabass (Dicentrarchus labrax).
Recently, several novel mycobacterial species such as M.
stephanolepidis, M. salmoniphilum, and M. sygnathidarum
have been isolated from diseased thread-sail filefish,
salmonid and sygnathid fish respectively [14].

records.rawDisplayText:
Other important bacterial fish pathogens
In recent times, certain bacteria with opportunistic
tendencies have been recognized as the primary factors
behind significant disease outbreaks in aquaculture settings
[25]. Some of the most notable fish pathogens among them
include Enterococcus faecalis, Piscirickettsia salmonis,
Renibacterium salmoninarum, Photobacterium damselae
subsp. Piscicida, Yersinia ruckeri, and Moritella viscosa,
which severely impact the aquaculture industry worldwide.
First observed in the yellow tail (Seriola quinqueradiata)
in Japan, Enterococcus spp. has been isolated from different
fishes such as tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) and turbot
(Scophthalmus maximus). Streptococcal infections in tilapia
caused by E. faecalis have been documented in Egyptian
and Thai lakes as well as from healthy and infected fish
from Bangladesh [26]. Piscirickettsiosis/Salmonid rickettsial
disease (SRS) attributed to Piscirickettsia salmonis stands
as a serious disease leading to huge economic setbacks
for the aquaculture sector. Initially isolated from infected
coho salmon, piscirickettsiosis has since then been found in
rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and Atlantic salmon
(Salmo salar). It has predominantly been documented in
marine and brackish ecosystems, with minimal occurrences
reported in freshwater environments [27]. Salmonid fish
are notably prone to an ailment referred to as bacterial
kidney disease (BKD), attributed to the fish pathogen
Renibacterium salmoninarum. Reported mortality rates
of approximately 80% and 40% have been documented in
pacific salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) and Atlantic salmon
(Salmo salar), respectively [28].
Photobacteriosis disease, caused by the Gram-negative
bacterium Photobacterium damselae subsp. piscicida,
afflicts a multitude of fish species, inducing a severe
septicemic condition observed in various warm water
marine fish species globally. It has been isolated from
economically important fish species, such as white perch
(Morone americanus), striped bass (Morone saxatilis),
sea bream (Sparus aurata), sole (Solea senegalensis and
Solea solea), cobia (Rachycentron canadum) and yellowtail
(Seriola quinqueradiata) primarily produced in China and
Japan, respectively and European sea bass (Dicentrarchus
labrax) cultured in Mediterranean countries [29]. Salmonids
(trout and salmon) and other cold-water fish are susceptible
to a bacterial infection called enteric redmouth disease
(ERM), also known as yersiniosis [30]. Additionally, it
has been found in other farmed fish hosts such as channel
catfish (Ictalurus punctatus), Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua
L.) as well as wild fish species [31]. The Gram-negative
bacterium, Moritella viscosa, causes winter ulcer disease,
which is characterised by massive, chronic ulcers in the skin
of different number of fish species. It is linked to cold marine
water conditions (i.e., below 10 °C) and results in significant,
persistent ulcers in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss),
halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus), Atlantic salmon
(Salmo salar), lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus), rainbow
trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), Halibut (Hippoglossus
hippoglossus), Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua), turbot
(Scophthalmus maximus) and Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua)
[32].

records.rawDisplayText:
The inadequacies of conventional methods
for identifying bacterial fish pathogens
Bacterial infections present substantial challenges to the
aquaculture sector, resulting in financial repercussions
and potential public health concerns. Accurate and
timely identification of fish pathogens is crucial for
effective disease management. Traditional techniques for
bacterial identification, such as culture-based methods
and biochemical tests, have traditionally found extensive
application in bacterial fish disease diagnosis in the past.
However, these techniques have several limitations that
hinder their effectiveness in providing accurate and timely
identification. The following are some of the key limitations
of traditional techniques:
• Slow and Time-Consuming: Traditional bacterial
identification methods often involve culturing the
pathogen on specific media and performing biochemical
tests, which can be time-consuming. It may take several
days or even weeks to obtain conclusive results, which
delays the diagnosis and subsequent implementation of
control measures [33].
• Limited Sensitivity: Some fish pathogens are fastidious
and require specific growth conditions, that pose challenges when attempting their isolation and identification
through conventional techniques. These methods might
fail to detect low levels of bacterial pathogens or identify
slow-growing or non-culturable strains [34], leading to
false-negative results.
• Limited Specificity: Traditional techniques rely on
phenotypic characteristics and biochemical reactions to
identify bacterial pathogens. However, some bacteria
may exhibit similar phenotypic features, leading to
misidentification or confusion between closely related
species. This can result in incorrect diagnoses and
inappropriate treatment strategies.
• Inability to Detect Mixed Infections: Bacterial fish
diseases can involve multiple pathogens, and traditional
techniques may fail to detect multiple bacterial species
in a single specimen [35]. This limitation hinders the
understanding of complex disease dynamics and may
lead to incomplete or inaccurate diagnosis.
• Lack of Genetic Information: Traditional techniques do
not provide comprehensive genetic information about
bacterial pathogens. This information is crucial for
understanding the virulence factors, genetic diversity,
and antimicrobial resistance profiles of bacterial fish
pathogens [36]. Without genetic data, it becomes
challenging to develop targeted control strategies and
monitor the emergence of new strains.
• Requirement for Culturable Organisms: Traditional
techniques heavily rely on the ability to culture the
bacteria in the laboratory [37]. However, some bacterial
species, especially unculturable or difficult-to-culture
strains, cannot be identified using these methods. This
limitation restricts the identification and characterization
of certain fish pathogens.

records.rawDisplayText:
These drawbacks have prompted the exploration of
genomics as an alternative approach for bacterial fish
pathogen study. These methods offer higher sensitivity,
specificity, and the ability to detect and characterize
pathogens directly from clinical samples, bypassing the
need for culture. They also provide valuable genotypic
information, enabling comprehensive analysis of bacterial
populations and facilitating the development of targeted
control measures [38].

records.rawDisplayText:
Genomic approaches for bacterial fish
pathogen identification and classification
High‑throughput sequencing in understanding
bacterial fish pathogen genomics
Genomic approaches have revolutionized the process of
identifying and categorizing bacterial fish pathogens by
providing comprehensive and accurate insights into their
genetic makeup. These approaches leverage high-throughput
sequencing technologies and advanced bioinformatics tools
to analyze the genomic data of pathogens, enabling rapid
and precise identification at various taxonomic levels [39]. A
very recent study employed the Illumina platform (MiSeq) to
ascertain the evolutionary relationships among the Shewanella
species obtained from fish specimens. The results of the
study indicate that, in contrast to the standard method of 16S
rRNA amplicon sequencing, which is considered the standard
approach, the use of whole-genome sequence (WGS) analysis
allowed for the taxonomic categorization and evaluation of the
diversity of the Shewanella spp. strains. This study indicates
that the species S. oncorhynchi, which was newly identified, is
the most commonly observed Shewanella species in freshwater
fishes [40].

records.rawDisplayText:
Whole‑genome sequencing (WGS) in bacterial fish
pathogen identification
Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) entails sequencing the
entire genome of a bacterial pathogen to reveal all its genetic
information. Researchers can correctly identify the pathogen
down to the species or strain level by comparing the derived
genomic sequence with reference databases. The discovery of virulence genes and other genomic factors linked to
pathogenicity is another benefit of WGS. The diversity and
evolutionary history of bacterial fish pathogens can be better
comprehended with the use of this data. Disease emergence
and spread can be monitored in both individual fish farms and
between farms using WGS, just as it can be done in hospitals
[41]. Many different bacterial pathogens found in aquaculture
have already had their complete reference genomes sequenced
which have been deposited by different regions around the
globe since 2004 (Fig. 2A). The data in (Fig. 2B) provides
insight into the temporal trends in the deposition of WGS of
bacterial fish pathogens, spanning from 2004 to July 2023,
showcasing the evolution of genomic research and data availability over the years.
